item.title: US-Iran nuclear talks collapse over scope and location dispute
item.description:
Scheduled nuclear negotiations between the United States and Iran fell apart Wednesday after Washington rejected Tehran's last-minute demands to move the talks from Istanbul to Oman and narrow their scope exclusively to nuclear issues, U.S. officials told Axios on February 4, 2026.

The breakdown came after Iran walked back previous agreements by insisting the Friday meeting take place in the Gulf state rather than Turkey, while also pushing for a purely bilateral format that would exclude discussions on ballistic missiles, regional proxies, and human rights.

"We told them it is this or nothing, and they said, 'Ok, then nothing,'" a senior U.S. official told Axios.

item.title: Study finds over 2,500 non-native plants could survive in Arctic
item.description:
A new study has identified more than 2,500 plant species that could potentially survive and establish themselves in the Arctic today, raising alarm about a looming ecological threat to one of Earth's most vulnerable ecosystems.

The research, published in the journal NeoBiota, found that 2,554 alien vascular plant species could find a suitable climatic niche in the Arctic tundra if transported there, with northern Norway emerging as a primary hotspot for potential invasions.

item.title: Saudi Arabia, Turkey sign deal for 5,000 MW of solar projects
item.description: Turkey and Saudi Arabia announced a sweeping expansion of economic and energy cooperation on Tuesday following Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's official visit to Riyadh, where he met with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman at Al-Yamamah Palace. The two countries issued a joint statement pledging to raise bilateral trade from its current level of more than $8.6 billion to $10 billion in the short term and $30 billion over the long term, while signing agreements to develop renewable energy projects and strengthen defense ties.

item.title: Oil prices surge as U.S.-Iran nuclear talks collapse
item.description:
Oil prices jumped more than 3% on Wednesday after reports emerged that planned nuclear talks between the United States and Iran have collapsed, reigniting fears of military conflict in the Middle East and potential disruptions to global oil supplies.

U.S. crude oil rose roughly 3.5% while global benchmark Brent climbed about 3.4% in afternoon trading, according to Investing.com. The sharp gains came after Axios reported that negotiations scheduled for Friday had been effectively canceled following a dispute over the location and scope of the discussions.

item.title: US-Iran nuclear talks back on after Arab leaders lobby Trump
item.description:
Scheduled nuclear negotiations between the United States and Iran appeared on the verge of collapse Wednesday before urgent appeals from at least nine Middle Eastern nations convinced the Trump administration to proceed with talks in Oman on Friday.

The diplomatic whiplash came after Iran demanded changes to both the venue and format of the meeting, initially planned for Istanbul. Tehran requested the talks be moved to Muscat and narrowed to a strictly bilateral format focused exclusively on nuclear issues, excluding discussions of ballistic missiles and regional proxy networks that Washington had sought to include.

item.title: US, EU, Japan forge critical minerals partnership to counter China
item.description:
The United States, European Union, and Japan announced a strategic partnership on Wednesday to bolster critical minerals supply chain security, marking a significant expansion of Western efforts to reduce dependence on Chinese-controlled materials vital to defense, technology, and clean energy industries.

The announcement came during the inaugural Critical Minerals Ministerial in Washington, which brought together delegations from over 50 countries. Secretary of State Marco Rubio hosted the summit, while Vice President JD Vance delivered opening remarks calling for a "preferential trade zone" protected by enforceable price floors.

item.title: Trump, Xi discuss soybean purchases, Taiwan arms in phone call
item.description: U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping spoke by phone on Wednesday in what Trump described as an "excellent" and "thorough" conversation, their first direct communication since late November. The wide-ranging call addressed trade, Taiwan arms sales, the Iran situation, and the Russia-Ukraine war as the two leaders prepare for Trump's planned visit to Beijing in April.

item.title: Coronal mass ejection reaches Earth, triggering minor storm watch
item.description:
A volatile sunspot region has erupted with dozens of powerful solar flares this week, causing radio blackouts across parts of the globe and sending charged particles hurtling toward Earth that could produce visible auroras in the coming days.

The culprit is sunspot region AR4366, which emerged on January 30 and has since grown into what scientists describe as a "solar flare factory," now spanning more than 15 Earth-widths across the sun's surface. Since February 1, the region has unleashed at least 64 solar flares, including five in the X-class—the most intense category—and more than 38 medium-sized M-class events.

The strongest eruption, an X8.1 flare that peaked at 11:57 p.m. UTC on February 1, was among the most powerful recorded during the current solar cycle. That blast triggered strong R3-level radio blackouts across the South Pacific, disrupting shortwave communications in eastern Australia and New Zealand, according to NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center.

item.title: Musk vows to launch 1 million satellites for AI data centers
item.description: Elon Musk announced this week that he wants to launch as many as a million satellites into orbit to form solar-powered data centers in space, aiming to meet the surging energy demands of artificial intelligence without straining Earth's power grids. But scientists and industry experts warn the world's richest man faces formidable technical, financial, and environmental obstacles.

item.title: Heavy snowfall cancels training as 2026 Winter Olympics open
item.description:
As the Milan-Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics prepare for their February 6 opening ceremony, organizers face a climate change paradox: decades of warming have left venues dependent on artificial snow, yet an intense last-minute snowfall has now forced the cancellation of training runs.

The 2026 Games are taking place in a much warmer climate than when Cortina d'Ampezzo last hosted in 1956, highlighting the growing challenge of staging winter sports in an era of rising global temperatures.

item.title: Oil surges as U.S.-Iran talks revived after near collapse
item.description: Oil prices jumped nearly 3 percent on Wednesday after nuclear talks between the United States and Iran briefly collapsed, before being revived following intense lobbying by Arab allies. The market swings underscored the fragility of diplomatic efforts to defuse tensions between Washington and Tehran amid a significant U.S. military buildup in the Middle East.

item.title: Last U.S.-Russia nuclear arms treaty set to expire Wednesday
item.description:
For the first time in over fifty years, the world's two largest nuclear powers will operate without limitations on their arsenals after the New START treaty expires on February 5, 2026. The lapse of the agreement, signed in 2010, marks the end of decades of arms control diplomacy between Washington and Moscow and raises concerns about a new era of nuclear competition that could also involve China.

The treaty, which capped deployed strategic warheads at 1,550 and delivery systems at 700 for each nation, also required on-site inspections and data exchanges—measures that had been suspended since Russia halted its participation following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

item.title: Engineers propose 50-mile seabed curtain to slow Thwaites melt
item.description:
A consortium of researchers and engineers is proposing to construct an 80-kilometer underwater barrier to shield Antarctica's Thwaites Glacier from the warm ocean currents driving its rapid deterioration. The ambitious Seabed Curtain Project comes as new data gathered from beneath the glacier reveals turbulent, warm waters capable of accelerating ice loss at an alarming rate.

The proposed structure would stand approximately 150 meters high and be anchored to the seabed at a depth of around 650 meters, forming a physical barrier to restrict the influx of warm water that is melting the glacier from below. The project aims to complete deployment by 2040, with an estimated construction cost of $40 to $80 billion and annual maintenance of $1 to $2 billion over its projected 25-year lifespan.

item.title: Oil prices fall as US and Iran confirm Friday talks in Oman
item.description:
Crude oil prices have swung sharply this week as military confrontations between the United States and Iran collided with diplomatic efforts, with markets reacting first to the collapse and then the revival of nuclear negotiations between Washington and Tehran.

West Texas Intermediate crude fell more than 1% on Thursday after the U.S. and Iran confirmed they will meet in Oman on Friday to discuss Iran's nuclear program, easing fears that recent hostilities could spiral into open conflict. The decline followed a roughly 3% surge the previous day, when the talks appeared on the verge of falling apart.

item.title: Oil prices dip as US and Iran confirm Friday talks in Oman
item.description:
Global oil prices fell on Wednesday evening as Washington and Tehran confirmed they would hold direct negotiations in Oman on Friday, easing fears of imminent conflict between the two nations.

U.S. crude slipped by about 1% to $64.50 per barrel in Asian trading late Wednesday, while Brent fell to approximately $68.49 per barrel, according to Reuters. The decline marked oil's first retreat in three days, following a 4.8% surge in the previous two sessions driven by fears of potential military strikes against the OPEC producer.

item.title: Gold tops $5,000 as weak jobs data fuels rate-cut hopes
item.description:
Gold reclaimed the key $5,000 level on Wednesday, climbing more than 1% to around $5,017 per ounce as safe-haven demand intensified amid rising geopolitical tensions and fresh signs of labor market softness in the United States. The rally marks a rebound for the precious metal after a volatile stretch that saw prices swing from a record high of nearly $5,595 late last month to a sharp plunge below $4,400 just days ago.

The surge comes as U.S. and Iranian officials confirmed high-stakes nuclear talks will take place Friday in Oman, with considerable uncertainty over whether the two sides can bridge wide gaps on Iran's nuclear program, ballistic missiles, and regional activities. Silver followed suit, jumping nearly 10% to around $91 per ounce.

item.title: UN chief calls New START expiration a 'grave moment'
item.description:
The New START treaty, the last remaining nuclear arms control agreement between the United States and Russia, expired at midnight GMT on Thursday, February 5, leaving the world without binding limits on the two largest nuclear arsenals for the first time in more than half a century.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the expiration "a grave moment for international peace and security" and urged both nations to return to the negotiating table without delay.

"For the first time in more than half a century, we face a world without any binding limits on the strategic nuclear arsenals of the Russian Federation and the United States of America—the two States that possess the overwhelming majority of the global stockpile of nuclear weapons," Guterres said in a statement released Wednesday.

item.title: Asian markets tumble as global tech selloff enters third day
item.description: Technology stocks extended a punishing selloff on Wednesday, with the Nasdaq Composite declining 1.5 percent for its worst two-day drop since last April's tariff-fueled turmoil. The global rout deepened as Asian markets followed Wall Street lower amid mounting concerns about artificial intelligence disruption and frothy valuations.

item.title: Volvo Cars Q4 profit tumbles 68% amid tariffs and weak demand
item.description: Volvo Cars reported a sharp decline in fourth-quarter profits on Thursday, blaming U.S. tariffs, weak consumer demand, and the removal of electric vehicle incentives for its struggles. Meanwhile, Toyota Motor Corporation is expected to report its third consecutive quarterly profit drop when it releases results this week, as rising costs and trade levies continue to pressure the world's largest automaker.

item.title: Nasdaq posts worst two-day drop since October amid AI fears
item.description:
A two-day rout in technology shares deepened Thursday as investors in Asia and Europe continued to flee the sector, spooked by fears over ballooning artificial intelligence investment costs and growing concerns that AI tools could disrupt the software industry.

The Nasdaq Composite recorded its worst two-day decline since October, breaching its 100-day moving average as selling extended from software makers into semiconductor stocks and other companies tied to AI infrastructure development. In Asia, the MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan tumbled 1.8%, weighed down by a 3.9% plunge in South Korea's Kospi and a 1.5% drop in Taiwan's Taiex.
